description: We are ORBIT – Beyond Earth, a team passionate about space exploration, science, and technology. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are developing an interactive space simulation game that allows young learners to manage a lunar or Martian outpost, make critical decisions, and balance limited resources. Our goal is to make real space engineering challenges engaging and understandable through gameplay. We value creativity, teamwork, and problem-solving.
summary:
Orbit is a pixel-art platformer, built in Godot, that teaches kids aged 7–12 the real trade-offs of deep space travel. Players guide an astronaut crew through three levels: a launch pad on Earth, the inside of a spacecraft in zero gravity, and a Moon base.
Every action costs something. More cargo needs more fuel, oxygen machines need power, and storm shields use up energy. Players also face real problems: lightning delays launches, CO2 builds up in the cabin, astronauts' muscles weaken without exercise, a solar storm sends the crew to a shelter, and the Moon's long night gives no sunlight for power.
It answers the challenge by turning real mission constraints into simple choices, with a short real fact after each one. Many children dream of being astronauts but learn little about space, and that interest fades. Learning by playing makes the knowledge stick.
The numbers are simplified for play, and the storm strengths are designed for the game. The facts come from NASA information, including its solar storm database.
details: Orbit is a 2d platformer game, that teaches kids aged 7–12, made in Godot 4. The player leads an astronaut crew through three levels: a launch pad on Earth, the inside of a spacecraft in zero gravity, and a Moon base. How it works: Every station shows its cost before the player presses E, so no choice is free. More cargo needs more fuel and more time. Oxygen machines need power. Shields protect against solar storms but use energy. Problems appear in each level: lightning delays the launch, a fuel leak drains the tank, CO2 builds up in the cabin, weak muscles hurt astronauts who skip exercise, a hull leak opens, and a solar storm gives a short countdown to reach the shelter. On the Moon, the long night gives no solar power. After each action the game shows one short real fact. Benefits and impact: Many children dream of space but learn little about how it works, and the interest fades. The game turns real mission constraints into simple choices that kids remember by playing. Each level builds on the one before, so the supplies players load at launch decide how well they survive later. Tools: Godot 4 (GDScript), Pixel art drawing app Creativity: The game is a learning story from Earth to the Moon, with different movement in each level (platforming, then floating in zero gravity). What we considered: Short text, simple controls, and facts checked against NASA pages. Game numbers are simplified, and storm strengths are designed for the game.
